description: Charles I's Personal Rule, the Civil War, the execution of a king and the restoration of monarchy.
content_html:
Charles I and Personal Rule 1629–1640

Charles I became king in 1625 and quickly clashed with Parliament over money and religion. Charles believed in the divine right of kings — the idea that his authority came directly from God, not from Parliament. Parliament, increasingly influenced by Puritan MPs, distrusted his religious policies (suspecting a Catholic drift) and his reliance on unpopular royal advisers such as the Duke of Buckingham.

In 1629, after Parliament passed a motion condemning his religious and financial policies while MPs physically held the Speaker in his chair, Charles dissolved Parliament and refused to call another. From 1629 to 1640 he governed without Parliament — a period known as the Personal Rule (also called the Eleven Years’ Tyranny by critics).

Key Fact

Charles I revived ship money in 1634 (for coastal towns) and extended it to inland counties in 1635. Without parliamentary approval, this was seen as an illegal tax. When John Hampden refused to pay in 1637, the resulting court case attracted national attention even though Charles technically won.

The Collapse of Personal Rule

Personal Rule ended when Charles’s attempt to impose a new Prayer Book on Scotland in 1637 provoked a Scottish rebellion (the Bishops’ Wars). To fund an army against the Scots, Charles had to call Parliament. The Short Parliament (April–May 1640) refused to grant money without addressing its grievances, so Charles dissolved it. The Long Parliament, called in November 1640, was determined not to be dismissed so easily.

The Long Parliament, led by John Pym, immediately moved to limit royal power: it abolished ship money, outlawed the Personal Rule’s courts, passed the Triennial Act (requiring Parliament to meet at least every three years), and — most remarkably — passed the Attainder of Strafford, forcing Charles to execute his own chief minister. By 1641, Charles had accepted more constraints on royal power than any previous English monarch.

Civil war erupted in 1642 when negotiations between Charles and Parliament broke down completely. In January 1642 Charles attempted to arrest five Members of Parliament for treason — including John Pym — but they had been tipped off and escaped. The attempt to use force against Parliament’s members was a constitutional outrage that alienated many who had previously supported the king.

The Civil War was not a simple conflict between royalists and parliamentarians. Religious, regional and social divisions cut across political ones. Many people tried to stay neutral. The Parliamentarians ultimately won because of the superior financial resources of London and the south-east, and the military reorganisation of their forces — culminating in the creation of the New Model Army in 1645.

Regicide and the Commonwealth

Charles I was captured, tried and executed on 30 January 1649. The trial was a constitutional revolution: a king charged by his own Parliament, convicted of making war on his own people, and executed publicly at Whitehall. The act of regicide shocked European courts and large parts of English opinion. Yet it also established, in the most dramatic way possible, the principle that monarchy was accountable.

Between 1649 and 1660 England was governed as a Commonwealth and then Protectorate. Oliver Cromwell served as Lord Protector from 1653 until his death in 1658. Parliament without a king proved unstable: Cromwell dissolved Parliament himself in 1653, ruling through a written constitution (the Instrument of Government) — ironically replicating some of the personal-rule problems he had fought against.

Key Fact

The execution of Charles I in 1649 was the most dramatic assertion that monarchy was accountable and could be removed. Even though monarchy was restored in 1660, no subsequent British monarch could ignore this precedent: the king could be killed if he governed tyrannically.

After Cromwell’s death, the various factions could not agree on a successor and General George Monck marched south to restore order. Charles II was invited back from exile in the Declaration of Breda (April 1660), in which he promised a general pardon, religious toleration, and to leave the settlement of disputed questions to Parliament. The Restoration was conditional — Parliament had dictated the terms.

The restored monarchy was constitutionally weaker than Charles I had claimed to be. Ship money was gone; the prerogative courts were gone; the Triennial Act was in force. Parliament expected to be consulted on taxation. The execution of Charles I had permanently altered what was politically possible: no Stuart king after 1660 could plausibly claim to govern without Parliament for long, as the crisis over James II would shortly demonstrate.
exam_tip_html: When writing about this period, always specify whether you mean the Civil Wars, the Commonwealth, or the Restoration — they are distinct phases. Also keep Charles I’s constitutional disputes distinct from Tudor ones: ship money and personal rule belong to Charles I (1629–40), not to the Tudors. A “Change and Continuity” essay on royal power across this period must address what changed after 1649 and what was restored in 1660 — it is not enough to say “Parliament won”; you need to say specifically what the changed balance of power looked like.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Charles I’s Personal Rule (1629–40) and the use of ship money were the immediate causes of the constitutional crisis that led to Civil War.
  • The execution of Charles I in 1649 established the principle that monarchy was accountable — no later British monarch could ignore this precedent.
  • The Restoration of 1660 brought monarchy back on Parliament’s terms — the prerogative courts, ship money and the right to govern without Parliament were gone permanently.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Charles I's Personal Rule (1629-1640).
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific feature (e.g. Charles I levied ship money without parliamentary consent) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. originally a coastal tax, he extended it to inland counties in 1635; when John Hampden refused payment in 1637, the resulting court case attracted national attention and damaged Charles's image). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to Charles governing without Parliament. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Long Parliament's actions against royal power in 1640-41.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. the Long Parliament abolished ship money — removing Charles's main non-parliamentary revenue source; the Triennial Act 1641 required Parliament to meet at least every three years — making it impossible for any future monarch to rule without Parliament for an extended period). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: one vague feature or irrelevant.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Charles I's attempt to arrest five Members of Parliament in January 1642 made civil war more likely.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (it was a constitutional outrage — using force against Parliament's members undermined the claim that Charles respected the rule of law; it failed — the MPs had been warned and escaped, humiliating the king; it confirmed parliamentary fears that Charles could not be trusted to keep agreements, making compromise impossible; it drove moderate MPs who had previously supported Charles into Parliament's camp, leaving him with a smaller royalist faction). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes the attempt without explaining why it accelerated war.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the execution of Charles I in 1649 was a significant turning point in the development of royal power.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (it established the principle that monarchy was accountable — a king could be tried and executed for making war on his own people; it set a precedent no later monarch could ignore — even after the Restoration in 1660 the threat of violent removal was real; it demonstrated that Parliament, if sufficiently determined, could override even the most fundamental constitutional convention; the Restoration itself confirmed the change — Charles II had to accept parliamentary conditions and the abolished prerogatives were not restored). Secure: two factors explained with relevant evidence. Developing: describes the execution as significant but does not explain the specific constitutional consequences. Emerging: describes the execution without addressing why it was a turning point.

practice_questions.text: How far did the period 1629-1660 permanently change the balance of power between the monarchy and Parliament? [You may consider: the Personal Rule; the execution of Charles I; the Restoration of 1660; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing both the scale of change (execution of a king; prerogative courts abolished; ship money gone; Triennial Act; Restoration on parliamentary terms) and the limits of that change (monarchy restored in 1660; Cromwell himself dissolved Parliament and ruled personally; the Instrument of Government was a quasi-monarchical document; James II would soon challenge the settlement again). Overall judgement about how permanent the change was, anchored in specific evidence. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes the constitutional changes accurately but does not weigh their permanence. Emerging: narrative of events without addressing the question of change.

practice_questions.text: Outline the main events that led from the outbreak of the Civil War in 1642 to the execution of Charles I in 1649.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points in sequence (Civil War breaks out 1642; Battle of Naseby 1645 — Parliamentarian victory; Charles surrenders to Scottish army 1646; Charles negotiates secretly with Scots 1647 — Second Civil War; Pride's Purge December 1648 removes moderate MPs; trial and execution of Charles I January 1649). Secure: two or three relevant points with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to Parliament defeating Charles.

knowledge_checks.q: What name is given to the period 1629-1640 during which Charles I governed without calling Parliament?
On what date was Charles I executed?
Ship money was originally a coastal tax but Charles I extended it to _____ counties in 1635, without parliamentary consent.
The _____ Act of 1641 required Parliament to be called at least every three years, preventing any future monarch from ruling without it for long.
Match each phase of government to its dates:

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Personal Rule and when did it last?
flashcard_questions.a: Charles I's government without Parliament, 1629-1640 (eleven years).

flashcard_questions.q: What was ship money and why was it controversial?
flashcard_questions.a: A tax extended to inland counties without parliamentary consent — widely seen as an illegal levy.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Triennial Act (1641) require?
flashcard_questions.a: Parliament to be called at least every three years, preventing extended personal rule.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Charles I executed and by whom?
flashcard_questions.a: 30 January 1649, by the authority of the Rump Parliament after a formal trial.
The killing of a reigning monarch by the state.

flashcard_questions.q: Who served as Lord Protector after the Civil War?
flashcard_questions.a: Oliver Cromwell, from 1653 until his death in 1658.

flashcard_questions.q: On what terms was Charles II restored to the throne in 1660?
flashcard_questions.a: He promised a general pardon, religious toleration, and to leave disputed matters to Parliament — the Restoration was conditional.

flashcard_questions.q: What attempt by Charles I in January 1642 made civil war more likely?
flashcard_questions.a: He attempted to arrest five Members of Parliament for treason — they escaped and the action alienated moderate opinion.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the New Model Army and why was it significant?
flashcard_questions.a: A reorganised Parliamentary army created in 1645 — it won the Civil War and later dominated politics, showing that military power underpinned political authority.

glossary_terms.definition: The eleven years from 1629 to 1640 during which Charles I governed without calling Parliament, funding his government through non-parliamentary means.
A traditional tax levied on coastal towns for naval defence, extended by Charles I to all counties from 1635 without parliamentary consent — a major cause of grievance.
The execution of a reigning monarch by the state — specifically used for the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649.
The republican government of England 1649-1660 — first as a republic (the Commonwealth) then under Oliver Cromwell's personal rule as Lord Protector (the Protectorate).
